text: Eisenhoit was called the German Benvenuto Cellini. He worked as a silver and gold smith, painter and engraver in Warburg. After years of apprenticeship and travel, he spent several years in Rome around 1590, working for a member of the papal curia. Back in Warburg he made artworks for twenty years, mostly commissions, such as pieces for the Metallotheca Vaticana by Michele Mercati. Some of his works have been ascribed to other masters.

Schindler was nicknamed Soldaten-Schindler, Soldier Schindler. His father, a painter and engraver, gave him his first lessons and encouraged his interest in military subjects. In 1836 he enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts, where Leopold Kupelwieser was one of his teachers. Later he took private lessons from his father's friend Peter Fendi, who introduced him to French military painters such as Hippolyte Bellangé and Nicolas Toussaint Charlet. He had his first exhibition at the academy in 1839, and he died of tuberculosis at twenty.

Skånberg was one of the first artists in Sweden to be influenced by Impressionism. Illness caused him great suffering, but he was prolific all the same. He was born out of wedlock in Norrköping to a maid, and a woman he called grandmother, Madame Juhlin, took care of him. A local tobacconist, who paid school tuition for children as a charity, helped him get an education. He died at thirty-two.

The younger brother of Albrecht Altdorfer, Erhard Altdorfer was most likely trained by him. They are believed to have started a workshop together in 1506. Around 1510 Erhard probably worked in Austria, at Lambach Abbey, St Florian and Klosterneuburg. In 1512 Duke Henry V of Mecklenburg-Schwerin appointed him court painter and architect in Schwerin, and he stayed there until his death. On a trip with the duke that year he probably met Lucas Cranach the Elder.

Fles was one of the first women admitted to the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam, along with Derkinderen-Besier, Grada Marius and Wally Moes. She studied with August Allebé and Anton Mauve. Afterwards she became interested in Impressionism and in the criticism of William Morris and John Ruskin. In 1900 she went to Paris to represent Arti et Amicitiae at the Exposition Universelle. She worked as an art critic as well as an artist.

Stuckenberg moved with his family from Munich to Delmenhorst near Bremen as a boy, where his father directed a linoleum factory. After unfinished architecture studies and art studies in Weimar and Munich, he spent five formative years in Paris, from 1907 to 1913. He made excursions to Pont-Aven and to Provence, where he cleaned his palette. He belonged to the circle of artists at the Café du Dôme. Back in Germany he lived in Berlin, where Herwarth Walden discovered him in 1916.

De Ferrari came to Genoa to study law but became a painter instead. He apprenticed with Domenico Fiasella from 1664 to 1669 and helped him on an altarpiece for the parish church in Montoggio. Then he spent four years in Parma, working on quadratura frescoes. There he gave up Fiasella's monumental style for a more lyrical one. He also copied Correggio's frescoes in the dome of Parma cathedral.

Ramboux's drawing teacher in Trier, Christoph Hawich, noticed his talent and recommended him to Jean-Henri Gilson, a former Benedictine monk who taught art in Florenville. After four years there another recommendation sent him to Jacques-Louis David in Paris, where he stayed until 1812. In 1815 he was admitted to the Royal Academy of Fine Arts as a pupil of Konrad Eberhard. The next year he moved to Rome. His father came from Savoy and his mother from a famous family of goldsmiths.

Bergmüller got his first training in his father's cabinet-making workshop in Türkheim. From 1702 to 1708 he was apprenticed to a court painter in Munich. In 1711 he made a cultural journey to the Netherlands, and later that year he became a master painter and a citizen of Augsburg. He married Barbara Kreutzerin, and they had ten children. One of them became a fresco painter too, as well as a copperplate engraver and art theorist.

Procaccini trained in the studio of Carlo Maratta and painted mostly religious works early in his career. His best-known altarpiece is Pope Pius V Triumphant over the Turks, in Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome. In 1718 he frescoed the prophet Daniel in the main nave of San Giovanni in Laterano. He also helped set up the papal factory for woven wall hangings. In 1720 Philip V of Spain went looking for an Italian portrait painter, and Procaccini then worked for the Spanish royal family for over a decade.

Houbraken says Dirck van Bergen was a pupil of Adriaen van de Velde and copied his style very well. He was popular. He spent his money as easily as he earned it. He spent some time in England but died in Haarlem, the city where he was born. According to the RKD his work later influenced Wilhelm von Kobell. Cows on a Footbridge is among his pictures.

A blacksmith's son from Besançon, Gigoux made his debut at the Salon in 1831. He became a contributor to Le Magasin pittoresque in 1833. Two years later he created several hundred woodcuts for Lesage's Gil Blas, which brought him a great deal of notoriety. In 1842 he was named a Chevalier in the Legion of Honour. He also collected art.

Mössmer began his artistic training in 1796 under Friedrich August Brand. As an instructor at the Vienna Academy he headed the landscape painting class for decades and encouraged painting outdoors. He exerted considerable influence without gaining much of a reputation for his own skill. His own landscapes are Neoclassical. His students included Emanuel Stöckler, August Heinrich, Anton Altmann and Friedrich Loos.

Cesare left Linköping at eighteen to study art in Paris, then went on to Buffalo, New York, to continue his studies. He moved to Chicago in 1903 and was living in Manhattan by 1911. One of his first jobs was illustrating The King of Gee-Whiz by Emerson Hough. His success as an illustrator got him into the Armory Show of 1913. He later worked for the Chicago Tribune, the New York World, the Sun and the Evening Post.

Royer volunteered for the Franco-Prussian War before his eighteenth birthday and fought at the Battle of Loigny-Poupry. General Charette noticed his artistic talent there and offered to pay for his studies at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. Royer became a pupil of Alexandre Cabanel and William-Adolphe Bouguereau, and he won the Prix de Rome in 1882. He became a portraitist and, above all, a painter of large scenes from the life of Joan of Arc in Domrémy.

Coffermans painted devotional panels and small altarpieces, and copies after painters of earlier generations. His idiom was old-fashioned, drawn from the Flemish Primitives such as Gerard David, Hugo van der Goes and Rogier van der Weyden, and from the prints of Martin Schongauer. His large Antwerp workshop exported many works to Spain and Portugal, where the old-fashioned style was much appreciated. Nobody knows for certain where or when he was born.

Mi Fu was known for a landscape technique later called Mi Dots, which used broad, wet ink dots applied with a flat brush. He was born in Taiyuan. He was also a poet and an art theorist. His poetry was influenced by Li Bai, while his calligraphy drew on Wang Xizhi. Scholars count him as one of the four major calligraphers of the Song dynasty, along with Su Shi, Huang Tingjian and Cai Xiang.

An apothecary's son from Foligno, Niccolò di Liberatore was known as L'Alunno. He was a pupil of Bartolomeo di Tomaso, whose assistant Benozzo Gozzoli brought a Florentine influence into his simple Umbrian feeling. His earliest known work, dated 1458, is in the Franciscan church of Deruta. He painted banners for religious processions as well as altarpieces. He died a rich man.

Flötner probably trained as a goldsmith in Augsburg with Adolf Daucher and contributed goldwork to the Fugger Chapel. After a stay in Italy he became a master craftsman in Ansbach, and later he moved to Nuremberg. He helped bring Italianate Renaissance design to sculpture and the decorative arts in Germany, in competition with the Vischer family. He worked in many media. Even so, he seems to have made only a modest living.

Contemporaries nicknamed Pietro Novelli the Raphael of Sicily. He was born in Monreale, which gave him the name il Monrealese, and he trained first with his father, a painter and mosaicist. In 1618 he moved to Palermo, where he apprenticed with Vito Carrera and studied perspective with the mathematician Carlo Maria Ventimiglia. His father died of the plague in 1625. His first dated work is from 1626.

Wu Li became a Catholic, and after he was widowed he joined the Society of Jesus. He studied for seven years at St. Paul's College in Macau and in 1688 was ordained at Nanjing as one of the first three Chinese Jesuit priests, taking the name Simon-Xavier a Cunha. For his last thirty years he served as a priest in rural villages. He painted landscapes, wrote poetry and practised calligraphy. He learned poetry from Qian Qianyi.

Zhou Wenju specialised in figure painting and worked as a painter in attendance at the Painting Academy of the Southern Tang court. He followed the Tang painter Zhou Fang. His birth and death dates are not known. Quite a few paintings are attributed to him, but none with much evidence. Most are later copies or misattributions. It is recorded that he took part in a joint work at a banquet held by Emperor Yuanzong on New Year's Day in 947.

A disciple of Francesco Francia, Pupini worked mainly in his native Bologna. He was active mostly between 1530 and 1540. He painted pictures for the church of San Giuliano, for the Basilica of San Giacomo Maggiore and for the church of Santa Maria della Baroncella. Among his works is a Madonna with Child, Saint Catherine, Saint Dominic and Saint Francis. Little else is recorded about him.

Brand's birth year is also given as 1693 or 1694. He was born in Frankfurt an der Oder, and his father soon moved the family business to Hamburg, where he finished his education. He then went to Regensburg to live with his mother's relatives and look for work in a commercial office. There he met the artist Christoph Ludwig Agricola and became interested in painting. Agricola mostly painted landscapes, so he pushed Brand in that direction.

Canuti trained in Bologna, first under Guido Reni and then under Guercino. He became a major painter of fresco decorations, and his ceilings mix Bolognese and Roman influences. Early in his career he made decorative works for the Palazzo Pepoli Campogrande in Bologna. By March 1665 he had finished his first commission there: two frescoes on the ceiling of the grand staircase, set in medallion-shaped stucco frames and showing events from the life of the 14th-century Bolognese figure Taddeo Pepoli.

Löfgren came from a Swedish-speaking Finnish family of merchants in Turku. His first art lessons came from a Norwegian-born drawing teacher named Legler, who with his friends convinced Löfgren's father to send the boy to Stockholm. He studied at the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts from 1842 to 1852 with Fredric Westin. In 1846 Robert Wilhelm Ekman got him a grant from the Finnish Art Association. He became a portrait painter.

The Dutch painter Felix Hess had work in the painting event of the art competition at the 1928 Summer Olympics. He studied at the Rijksakademie van beeldende kunsten in Amsterdam and belonged to Arti et Amicitiae. In 1939 his work was also part of the exhibition and sale Onze Kunst van Heden at the Rijksmuseum. He was killed in the Sobibor extermination camp during World War II.

The son of a painter, Domenico, Peruzzini was born in Ancona in 1643 or 1646. His landscapes show the influence of Salvator Rosa, and of Dutch landscape artists popular in Italy. His works often included capricci, like those of Marco Ricci. He stayed in Bologna for four years in the 1680s and worked there with Sebastiano Ricci and Giovanni Antonio Burrini. He travelled widely.

Bellermann's father, a tanner, died young, and as the eldest child he helped care for the family, working as a sheep herder until his talent was discovered. At fourteen he entered the Weimar drawing school to become a porcelain painter, but vision problems sent him home to Erfurt. In 1840 he travelled to Norway with Friedrich Preller, and the large canvas he painted afterward showed his skill at accurately representing nature. King Frederick William IV bought it. It is now lost. Alexander von Humboldt then recommended him for an expedition to Venezuela, where he stayed from 1842 to 1845.
